title: example · how Spec:parse splits into two phases

steps.title: parse = normalize + resolve
steps.brief: two phases: emit fragments, then fold them
steps.body: normalize() walks your tables and emits FRAGMENTS. meta:resolve() folds fragments into PLUGINS. Nothing is loaded; this is pure data.

detail.t: Two phases separated by a hard boundary. Phase one is syntactic: it cares only how your tables nest. Phase two is semantic: identity, inheritance and pruning all appear there.

detail.c:
function Spec:parse(spec)
  self:normalize(spec)   -- syntax  -> fragments
  self.meta:resolve()    -- meaning -> plugins
end

detail.t: Almost every surprising behaviour becomes obvious once you ask which phase it belongs to. "Why did my two specs merge?" is phase two.

steps.title: ★ frag_stack vs dep_stack
steps.brief: ★ dep_stack is what turns nesting into an edge
steps.body: Both `dependencies` and `specs` create child fragments. Only `dependencies` also pushes dep_stack — the whole difference between nested and depended-upon.

detail.t: Two stacks answering two different questions. frag_stack answers "who contains me". dep_stack answers "who is currently collecting dependencies".

detail.c:
did = top(dep_stack)
if did and did == pid:     -- parent is collecting
  frag.dep = true
  parent.deps += id        -- the edge, as an ID
push frag_stack, id
if plugin.dependencies:
  push dep_stack, id       -- ONLY here
  normalize(dependencies)
  pop dep_stack

detail.t: `did == pid` is the whole trick. dep_stack is honoured only when its top is my DIRECT parent, which stops a grandchild inside a nested `specs` from being registered as a dependency of the grandparent.

ann.text: ★ The whole difference between `dependencies` and `specs` lives in the next twenty lines.
